THE SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1917.
THE PASSPORTS CASE.
Made by
Final Stage Reached.
INTERESTING ARGUMENTS.
The two remaining defendants in the passports case were brought before Mr. Byrne, British Assessor, and Magistrate Kwan, at the Mixed Court at 11.30 o'clock yesterday morning. The session, which lasted well over two hours, was occupied with the hearing of argument by Counsel engaged in the case.
Mr. Salmon, summing up, said in view of the serious public interest in the passport question one could fully understand why the prosecution and the Police were so keen to sift this business to the bottom but unfortunately there might be a natural tendency in their zeal which would subconsciously lead them to indulge in wild theories and speculation and also to be, he would not say vindictive, but rather hard and eager. In the course of his conduct of his case, Counsel for the prosecution, for whose general sense of fairness and moderation he yielded to none, had discussed loosely and light-heartedly on a question of law, such as collective responsibility and criminal negligence under the Chinese Provisional Code to justify the Court to punish the master for the acts of his servants.
What was this collective responsibility Counsel asked. It was the first time, he had to admit, even in that Court, to have heard it was to be applied to felonies and serious crime. Counsel asked if they were to punish the head of a family for the crime of a member of a family.
Kindler Scored.
"It is my unpleasant duty also to refer to Kindler," Mr. Salmon continued. "This man is not only an accomplice but is the fons et origo of the whole thing. It was in his brains that the plot was hatched. It was he who got the deluded and misguided Chinese into his meshes. I don't wish to be uncharitable to the man. Kindler told us that he did this because he had received a hint, not more than a hint, that his business might be boycotted if he did not do as the Germans wanted. A man with a little moral strength would have refused to act from such a motive even if his business were to be affected in the way threatened. There must be something wrong in the moral character of that man. Even if he had said that he did this for his country's good and for a patriotic purpose, however much we may differ with him, and how much we can hope that his scheme may be frustrated, still we cannot help but have a little respect for him. But under the circumstances all respect is taken from him.
"He also told us that when in the presence of the Police and in Court he makes it a point to speak the truth: presumably on other occasions truth is allowed to go to the four winds."
The Two Hours Hint.
It was required at law that the evidence of an accomplice must be corroborated, Counsel went on, and if there was anything liable to favourable construction for the accused, that construction should be adopted. But the circumstances were such that the Court should deal very cautiously with this evidence. Kindler said he visited the shop at 8 p.m., after office hours, but previous to that he had been around town for two or three hours. Why did he not go to the shop at a reasonable hour? What took place during those two hours? What conspiracy might not have been hatched? And who might not have been taken into the secret?
Counsel then dealt with the manner by which Kindler gave the order. He said it was in a backroom, but why did he not address himself to the management or some other responsible person in the shop. There was no evidence whatever that the press was directly or indirectly connected with the crime. The Police had not found a single block connected with the printing of the passports.
Question of Guilty Knowledge.
Counsel submitted that guilty knowledge must be proved to exist at the time the offence was committed. If they knew afterwards that what they had done was an offence and that therefore it was improper, and took steps to protect themselves, they may be charged with not helping the police or with not giving testimony. But the principal offence could not stand unless guilty knowledge was proved to exist in their minds at the time the offence was committed. Counsel then quoted law dealing with the point of accessory after the fact.
In conclusion, Mr. Salmon asked the Court before condemning his client to weigh the evidence very carefully and to give the benefit of any reasonable doubt to the accused, and whenever possible to construe his conversation, his action and his demeanour

有趣的辩论。
昨日（星期一）上午11时30分，护照案中剩余的两名被告被提审至会审公廨，由英国陪审官拜恩先生（Mr. Byrne）和关谳员（Magistrate Kwan）审理。庭审持续了两个多小时，主要用于听取本案辩护律师的辩论意见。

萨尔蒙先生（Mr. Salmon）在总结陈词中表示，鉴于公众对护照问题的高度关注，完全可以理解检方和警方为何如此热衷于将此案查个水落石出；但不幸的是，他们的热情中可能存在一种自然倾向，会在潜意识里导致他们沉溺于荒诞的理论和猜测，并且——他不愿说是出于报复心理——而是表现得过于严厉和急切。他在陈述案件过程中指出，尽管他对控方律师普遍具有的公平感和克制精神极为推崇，但后者却轻率且漫不经心地讨论了一个法律问题，即依据《中华民国暂行新刑律》中的集体责任和刑事过失概念，来证明法庭有权因仆役的行为而惩罚主人，这种做法是站不住脚的。

萨尔蒙律师问道，什么是集体责任？他承认，即便是在这个法庭上，这也是他第一次听到将集体责任应用于重罪和严重犯罪。他反问，难道要因为家庭成员的罪行而惩罚一家之主吗？

金德勒受到抨击。
萨尔蒙先生继续说道：“我也不得不令人不快地提及金德勒（Kindler）。此人不仅是共犯，更是整个事件的始作俑者（fons et origo）。阴谋正是在他的脑海中策划出来的。正是他将那些受蒙蔽和误导的中国人罗织进他的圈套。我不愿对这个人刻薄。金德勒告诉我们，他这样做是因为收到了一丝暗示——仅仅是一丝暗示——如果他不按照德国人的意愿行事，他的生意可能会遭到抵制。一个稍有道德定力的人，即使面临生意受威胁的后果，也会拒绝出于这种动机行事。那个人的道德品格一定有问题。即便他说他是为了国家利益和爱国目的才这样做，无论我们与他有多大的分歧，无论我们多么希望他的计划落空，我们仍不禁会对他产生一丝敬意。但在目前的情况下，他对他的所有尊重都荡然无存。

“他还告诉我们，当他在警察面前和在法庭上时，他特意坚持讲真话：这大概意味着在其他场合，真话就被抛到九霄云外去了。”

两小时的暗示。
辩护律师接着指出，法律规定共犯的证词必须有佐证，如果有任何有利于被告的解释，应当采纳这种解释。但鉴于具体情况，法庭在处理此类证词时应非常谨慎。金德勒说他是在晚上8点，即下班后访问了该店铺，但在此之前，他已在城里逛了两三个小时。他为什么不在合理的时间去店铺？在那两个小时里发生了什么？可能策划了什么阴谋？又有谁可能被拉入秘密之中？

随后，辩护律师讨论了金德勒下达命令的方式。他说那是在一间后屋里进行的，但他为什么不直接找店里的管理层或其他负责人呢？没有任何证据表明印刷厂与犯罪行为有直接或间接的联系。警方并未发现任何一块与护照印刷有关的印版。

明知故犯的问题。
辩护律师提出，必须证明在犯罪发生时存在“明知故犯”的心理状态。如果他们事后才知道自己的行为是犯罪，因而是不当的，并采取措施保护自己，他们可能会被指控不协助警方或不提供证词。但是，除非能证明在犯罪发生时他们心中存在明知故犯的心理，否则主要罪名不能成立。随后，辩护律师引用了关于事后从犯的法律条文。

最后，萨尔蒙先生请求法庭在谴责其当事人之前仔细权衡证据，给予被告任何合理怀疑的利益，并在可能的情况下，将其在证人席上的谈话、行为和举止解释为与其无罪相一致。对他没有任何证据。

REPOR Mr. Newman, replying, said his
learned friend had left out the point
which the prosecution intended to urge
on the Court—that of an accessory
after the fact. Counsel admitted there
was not sufficient evidence to convict
Made by the man of the actual forging of the orwa
document, although there might be
strong suspicion.
Mr. Newman referred to the criminal
negligence of the accused in purposely
not conducting inquiries into the
sources of the order such as any cautious
business man would do. Why were not
the accountant and the shroff at the
printing works called for the
defence? The excessive price charged
was the strongest evidence of their
guilty knowledge the prosecution could
offer. The shroff knew and yet he was
not called. The Police admit that
this work was not with any deep
criminal intention, the men did not
really and properly understand the
importance of their criminal act.
Mr. Newman said he was not there
to defend Kindler in any shape or form
but he must say that what Kindler had
told them about his visits to May
Sun and other places was quite true.
The Police searched for Kindler's
name in the books of the printing
company but they would have been
extremely surprised if they had found
it. It was not likely, for in case of
trouble it would be found in the books.
He suggested that the money received
for the printing of the documents must
have been simply divided amongst the
persons who were cognisant of the
offence. It would, of course, be im-
possible to prove, but each man must
have actually received a portion.
Counsel also drew the Court's
attention to the attitude adopted by
Mr. Salmon's client and his reticence,
refusing to give the Police any in-
formation whatever. He also denied
that the printing had been done there.
May Raise International Complications.
Mr. Newman continued: "These
people must exercise a reasonable
amount of care in accepting work like
this. It may implicate persons of all
sorts, and it may raise international
complications between China and the
various countries whose neutrality has
been endangered in that way. It was
a most serious offence but in fairness to
the accused I must say that they did not
realise it, but it must be shown to others
in future that they must realise the
danger of printing public documents
such as these without first obtaining a
proper authority from persons who are
able to give the order for such printing.

"The fear of a penalty overhanging
their heads will make it difficult and
not worth their while for those who are
in a position to carry out such work, to
run the risk to make a little extra
money by the printing of such
documents."
With regard to the Honan Road
man, Counsel said the man's guilt or
innocence solely depended on what the
opinion of the Court was, and the
amount of guilty knowledge he had
when he did make those seals for the
passports. There was one strong piece
of evidence against him: he was told
by another printer that he would have
first to obtain a proper authority to
make the seals. Counsel said he was of
opinion that the man knew that what
he was doing was something wrong, but
he did not care what it was.
Dentistry and Passports.
Mr. Priestwood, summing up the case
for his client, mentioned the fact that
when Det. Sergt. Givens went to the
Honan Road shop to search and exa-
mine the books, they found an impres-
sion of a Norwegian Consulate seal
in one of the books kept as a record.
It was not likely, Counsel pointed out,
that the man if he knew that when he
made the seals he was doing wrong,
would keep a record of an impression
which, when found, would incriminate
him.
Mr. Priestwood continued: "Whether
Mr. Kindler admits it or not, I say he
was a secret agent of the German
government. Mr. Salmon the other
day asked Kindler what connection
there was between dentistry and
passports, and he had answered there
was none. But there is, I submit. It
was the cleverest position they could
think of, and the fact that he was a
dentist was the very reason why he
was selected by the Germans because of
his position in the Settlement, and be-
cause of the ease with which they could
deceive the Chinese. We have been told
that when a German does a thing he
does it well; and is it very difficult
to understand that a man in Kindler's
position would find it easy to deceive
these men? It would be shocking in
all conscience to have these Chinese
punished when Kindler should go
free—"
The Assessor: He turned King's
evidence.
Mr. Priestwood: That is from the
legal point of view. I am speaking from
the ethical viewpoint, and I say that it
would be shocking to all conscience if
these poor Chinese should be convicted
and a foreigner, that is, Kindler, who
instigated the whole thing, goes free."
In conclusion, Counsel said he left the
case with all confidence in the hands of
the Court.
Judgment was reserved.

记者报道：纽曼先生（Mr. Newman）在答复时说，他的博学的朋友遗漏了检方打算向法庭强调的一点——即事后从犯的问题。辩护律师承认，虽然没有足够的证据定罪该人实际伪造文件，尽管可能有强烈的嫌疑。

纽曼先生提到了被告的刑事过失，即故意不对订单来源进行调查，而任何谨慎的商人都会这样做。为什么印刷厂的会计师和收银员（shroff）没有被传唤为辩方作证？收取的高额费用是检方能提供的证明他们明知故犯的最有力证据。收银员知情，但他未被传唤。警方承认，这项工作并非带有深层的犯罪意图，这些人并没有真正和充分地理解其犯罪行为的严重性。

纽曼先生说，他不是为了以任何形式为金德勒辩护，但他必须说，金德勒告诉他们的关于他访问梅孙（May Sun，音译）和其他地方的情况完全是真实的。警方在印刷公司的账簿中搜寻金德勒的名字，但如果他们找到了，那才会令他们极度惊讶。这不太可能，因为一旦出事，名字就会出现在账簿上。他暗示，用于印刷文件的钱肯定只是在那些知晓罪行的人之间进行了分配。当然，这无法证明，但每个人肯定实际收到了一份。

辩护律师还提请法庭注意萨尔蒙先生当事人的态度及其缄默，拒绝向警方提供任何信息。他还否认印刷工作是在那里完成的。

可能引发国际纠纷。
纽曼先生继续说道：“这些人在接受此类工作时必须行使合理的注意义务。这可能牵连各类人员，并可能引发中国与其中立地位因此受到危及的各个国家之间的国际纠纷。这是一项非常严重的罪行，但出于对被告的公平，我必须说他们并没有意识到这一点，但必须向其他人表明，未来他们在未首先从有权下达此类印刷命令的人员处获得适当授权的情况下，必须认识到印刷此类公共文件的危险。

“对惩罚的恐惧悬在他们头顶，将使那些有能力执行此类工作的人觉得，为了通过印刷此类文件赚取一点额外收入而冒险，既困难又不值得。”

关于河南路的那名男子，辩护律师说，该人的有罪或无罪完全取决于法庭的看法，以及他在制作护照印章时所拥有的明知故犯的程度。有一条对他不利的有力证据：另一名印刷工告诉他，他必须首先获得适当的授权才能制作印章。辩护律师说，他认为此人知道自己在做坏事，但他不在乎那是什么。

牙科与护照。
普里斯特伍德先生（Mr. Priestwood）为其当事人总结案情时提到，当警佐吉文斯（Det. Sergt. Givens）前往河南路的店铺搜查并检查账簿时，他们在作为记录保存的一本账簿中发现了挪威领事馆印章的印模。辩护律师指出，如果此人知道制作印章是做错事，他不太可能保留一份一旦发现就会使他获罪的印模记录。

普里斯特伍德先生继续说道：“无论金德勒先生是否承认，我说他是德国政府的秘密特工。前几天萨尔蒙先生问金德勒，牙科和护照之间有什么联系，他回答说没有。但我认为有联系。这是他们能想到的最巧妙的位置，而他是一名牙医的事实正是他被德国人选中的原因，因为他在租界的地位，以及因为他们可以轻易地欺骗中国人。有人告诉我们，德国人做事做得很好；难道很难理解像金德勒这样地位的人会很容易欺骗这些人吗？如果金德勒逍遥法外，而这些中国人受到惩罚，那真是违背良心令人震惊——”

陪审官：他转为王室证人（指转为控方证人）。

普里斯特伍德先生：那是从法律角度来看的。我是从道德角度来讲的，我说，如果这些可怜的中国人被判有罪，而煽动整个事件的外国人，即金德勒，却逍遥法外，那将是违背所有良心的令人震惊之事。”

最后，辩护律师表示，他充满信心地将此案交由法庭裁决。
判决保留。

THE PASSPORT CASE.
Judgment.
Judgment in the Passport Case was delivered by British Assessor Byrne, and Magistrate Kwan, in the Mixed Court yesterday.
Mr. K. E. Newman appeared for the prosecution, Mr. J. G. Priestwood, Mr. W. S. Fleming, and Mr. J. E. Salmon for the defence.
The Assessor, in delivering his decision said :—These prosecutions have their origin in the sinister activities of certain individuals who have since translated to other parts. Too long had they abused the neutrality of China for the furtherance of their scheme as belligerents and to the prejudice of China and its people! After the experience that three years of a terrible war have given to the world it is unnecessary perhaps to emphasise here the serious consequences that result from the making of spurious passports —what loss of life and treasure may we not attribute to the handiwork of wretched instruments of craft in the case! However we are convinced that the Chinese implicated in these forgeries were not fully conscious of the serious nature of the acts they did and consequently we do not see our way to visit them with the punishment that would be theirs if a clearer understanding of their position had been present to their minds. They were then not altogether ignorant tools of a man who seems not to have been entirely a free agent.
The revelations made in the course of this case should have the effect of deterring any reckless Chinese or foreigners of what condition soever in the settlement from inter-meddling with transactions susceptible of being turned to political use.
You prisoner, Lob, are an old workman, and we go so far as to say that you have hitherto been a capable and an honest one. It is clear to us that you were not able to withstand the inducement held out to you to make a petty gain. And you wilfully closed your eyes to what you must have known to be the criminal side of your conduct in making the seals and procuring to be made the documents mentioned in the evidence adduced against you. As you stand before us in the dock at the close of a laborious and useful life we cannot but feel pity for your age and infirmities. We will deal with you as leniently as possible in sentencing you
to a term of four months' imprisonment from the date of your arrest.
You prisoner, Yang, fortunately for yourself do not appear to have come into personal contact with the emissary Kindler. We are convinced that the passports were lithographed in your printing establishment, and the fact of their having been so lithographed must, from your re-iterated statements in the witness box, have come to your knowledge, if not during the process of their manufacture at least soon after their completion. Yet you denied all knowledge of this transaction, and various employees of yours, under your control, made a like denial—it was significantly described by the police officer as half-hearted. You have not shown any signs of contrition, and in fact we are of opinion that most of your evidence is unworthy of belief. We have some doubt as to your being a principal in the commission of the forgery, but not any doubt as to your being an accessory after the fact. Doubtless the grievous character of your offence has been by this time brought home sufficiently to you, and we therefore order you to pay a fine of $800 and to enter into your own recognisance in the sum of $1,000 to be of good behaviour for two years.
Mr. Priestwood made application under article 63 of the Chinese Criminal Code for a postponement of punishment. He pointed out that his client had been in custody since September 1.
The Assessor: We have taken all the circumstances into consideration, and we consider that we have dealt exceedingly leniently with your client in sentencing him to a term of four months.

护照案。
判决。
护照案之判决由英国陪审官拜恩（Byrne）与关谳员（Magistrate Kwan）于昨日在会审公廨宣判。
纽曼（K. E. Newman）先生代表控方出庭，普里斯特伍德（J. G. Priestwood）先生、弗莱明（W. S. Fleming）先生及萨尔蒙（J. E. Salmon）先生代表辩方出庭。
陪审官在宣读判决时称：——这些起诉源于某些个人的阴险活动，这些人此后已转移至其他地区。他们以交战国身份滥用中国之中立地位以推进其阴谋，损害中国及其人民利益，为时已久！在世界经历了三年惨痛战争之后，或许无需在此强调伪造护照所导致的严重后果——我们岂能将生命与财产的损失不归咎于本案中那些狡猾之徒的卑劣行径！然而，我们确信，卷入这些伪造活动的中国人并未充分意识到其行为性质的严重性，因此，我们认为若他们对其处境有更清晰的认识，本应受到更严厉的惩罚，但鉴于此，我们无法对他们施以那样的刑罚。他们并非完全无知，只是被一个似乎并非完全拥有自由意志的人所利用的工具。
本案审理过程中所揭露的事实，应能起到震慑作用，使租界内任何鲁莽的中国人或外国人，无论其身份如何，不再插手那些可能被用于政治目的的交易。
被告洛布（Lob），你是一名老工匠，我们甚至可以说，你迄今为止一直是一名能干且诚实的工匠。显然，你未能抵挡住诱使你谋取微利的诱惑。你故意对你必定知晓的犯罪行为视而不见，即制作印章并 procuring（获取/安排制作）证据中提及的文件。当你站在被告席上，结束了一生辛劳且有益的工作时，我们不禁对你的年迈和体弱感到怜悯。在量刑时，我们将尽可能从宽处理，判处你自被捕之日起监禁四个月。
被告杨（Yang），对你而言幸运的是，你似乎并未与代理人金德勒（Kindler）有过个人接触。我们确信，护照是在你的印刷所内石印的，而且根据你在证人席上一再陈述的情况，即使不在制造过程中，至少在完成之后不久，你也必然知晓此事。然而，你否认对此交易有任何了解，而你控制下的多名雇员也作了同样的否认——正如警官所指出的那样，这种否认显得并不坚决。你未表现出任何悔意，事实上，我们认为你的大部分证词不值得采信。对于你是否为伪造案的主犯，我们尚存疑虑；但对于你是事后从犯，则毫无疑问。无疑，你罪行之严重性至此已足以让你深刻体会，因此，我们命令你缴纳罚款 800 元，并具结保释金 1,000 元，保证在两年内行为良好。
普里斯特伍德先生依据《中华民国刑法》第六十三条申请暂缓量刑。他指出，其当事人自 9 月 1 日起一直被羁押。
陪审官：我们已考虑所有情节，并认为在判处你当事人四个月监禁时，我们已经极为从宽。
